objectives: Explain what a token is and why models see ids not text
Describe how embeddings map ids to vectors

slides.title: Part 1 — Why text must become numbers
slides.body: A neural network is a pipeline of differentiable tensor operations. It has no notion of a letter. The very first design decision in any language model — how to turn a string into numbers — quietly determines cost, capability, and a surprising number of famous failures.

slides.title: The model only ever sees vectors
slides.body:
The fixed pipeline, end to end:

`raw text  →  tokens  →  integer ids  →  embedding vectors  →  the model`

A **tokenizer** is a deterministic function `str → int[]`: it segments the string into *tokens* and maps each to an integer id in a fixed **vocabulary** $V$ (e.g. $|V|=50{,}000$). An **embedding table** $E\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d}$ — a learned matrix — turns each id into a dense vector via a row lookup $E[\text{id}]$. From the transformer's perspective the input is *only* that matrix of vectors; it never sees characters again. Two artifacts ship with every model: the tokenizer (vocab + merge rules) and $E$. Swap the tokenizer and every id — and all of $E$ — is invalidated.

slides.title: Why not the obvious options
slides.body:
Two naive tokenizations, each fatally lopsided:

**Character-level.** Vocabulary is tiny (~100 symbols) and nothing is ever out-of-vocab. But sequences are *long*: "transformer" → 11 tokens. Since self-attention is $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ in sequence length $n$, long sequences are quadratically expensive, and the model must relearn spelling from scratch before it can learn meaning.

**Word-level.** Sequences are short and semantically clean, but the vocabulary is unbounded — every name, typo, compound, and inflection is a distinct word. You must cap it, and every word outside the cap collapses to a single `<unk>` token: information *destroyed* before learning begins. Morphology ("run/runs/running") is lost — each is an unrelated id.

**Subword** tokenization (BPE — next lesson) is the engineered compromise: frequent words stay whole, rare words decompose into reusable pieces, and nothing is ever `<unk>`. Understanding *why* the extremes fail is what makes BPE's design feel inevitable.

slides.title: The sequence-length tax — quantified
slides.body: Every token costs compute and one slot of the finite context window, and attention cost scales **quadratically**. Concretely: tokenizer A encodes a document in 1,000 tokens; tokenizer B (worse fit) in 1,300. The attention term scales like $n^2$, so B costs $(1300/1000)^2\approx 1.7\times$ as much *for the same text*, and exhausts a fixed context budget ~30% sooner. Tokenization is therefore a **latency, cost, and context-length decision**, not mere preprocessing — which is exactly why frontier labs invest heavily in tokenizer quality.

slides.title: Ids are labels, not magnitudes
slides.body: Token id 5,000 is not "twice" id 2,500 and not "near" id 5,001 — ids are arbitrary labels assigned by vocabulary construction order. Feeding the integer directly would inject a meaningless ordinal signal. That's the entire reason for the embedding table: each id indexes a *learned* vector, and similar tokens acquire similar vectors **because training moved them there**, not because their ids are close. The embedding is where "king − man + woman ≈ queen"-style structure can even exist; raw ids could never encode it.

slides.title: Part 2 — Worked examples & the subtleties that bite
Worked example: encode a sentence
slides.body: Take "unhappiness" under a subword vocab that learned the pieces `un`, `happy`, `ness` but not the whole word. Encoding: `un` `happy` `ness` → e.g. ids `[412, 9981, 530]` → three embedding rows $E[412],E[9981],E[530]$ → a $3\times d$ matrix. A word-level tokenizer that never saw "unhappiness" would emit `[<unk>]` — one row, all morphology gone. Subword keeps the model able to relate "unhappiness" to "happy" and "happiness" through shared pieces. This is the concrete payoff of the compromise.

slides.title: Whitespace, case, and the leading space
slides.body: Modern tokenizers attach the leading space to the *following* token, so `" cat"` and `"cat"` are **different ids**. Case usually matters too (`Cat` ≠ `cat`) unless the tokenizer lowercases. Consequence: a stray leading/trailing space in a prompt changes the token sequence and therefore the model's behavior — the source of countless "why did the same prompt act differently?" mysteries. Pros inspect the actual token ids when debugging prompt sensitivity rather than trusting the visible text.

slides.title: Numbers and code tokenize badly — and why
slides.body: BPE merges are learned from a mostly-prose corpus, so digit strings and code punctuation are *rare pairs* and stay fragmented: `12345` might split `123|45`, and code like `arr[i]+=1` shatters into many tiny tokens. Two real consequences: (1) early LLMs were poor at arithmetic substantially because a number had no stable representation across contexts; (2) code models adopt code-aware tokenizers. The lesson: a model's apparent reasoning failure is sometimes a *tokenization* failure upstream of any reasoning.

question.question: A word-level tokenizer is trained, then deployed. A user types a brand-new product name it never saw. What happens?
options: It is mapped to a single special "unknown" token, losing all information in that name
The tokenizer invents a new vocabulary entry on the fly
The model reads it character by character automatically
question.explanation: A pure word tokenizer has a vocabulary fixed at training time. Anything unseen collapses to a single `<unk>` token — the model literally cannot tell one unknown word from another. This out-of-vocabulary failure is the core reason subword tokenization replaced word tokenization.

question.question: Tokenizer A averages 4 characters/token; tokenizer B averages 2 characters/token. For the same document, roughly how does B's self-attention compute compare to A's?
options: About 4× more (cost grows with the square of token count)
The same — attention cost doesn't depend on the tokenizer
About half (fewer characters per token is cheaper)
question.explanation: B produces 2× as many tokens for the same text (half the characters per token). Self-attention is O(n²) in the token count, so doubling n quadruples that term: (2n)² / n² = 4×. Token efficiency is a real architectural lever, not a cosmetic detail.

question.question: Order these from FEWEST to MOST tokens produced for the same 500-word English paragraph.
question.explanation: Word-level emits roughly one token per word (~500). Subword splits some rare words into 2–3 pieces, so it is a bit higher (~650). Character-level emits one token per character (~2,800). Fewer tokens means shorter sequences and cheaper attention — but word-level pays for it with the out-of-vocabulary problem, which is why subword wins in practice.

slides.title: Tokenization and embedding, precisely
slides.body: Formally: tokenization is a function $\tau:\Sigma^{*}\to V^{*}$ from strings over an alphabet to sequences over the vocabulary; embedding is $\varepsilon:V\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ realized as a lookup into the trainable matrix $E$. The model is $f(\varepsilon(\tau(\text{text})))$. $\tau$ is fixed (not learned) and *invertible enough* to detokenize; $\varepsilon$ (the matrix $E$) **is** learned jointly with the rest of the network by backprop, exactly like any other weight. Reconstruct this pipeline and its invariants:

slides.title: Part 4 — Edge cases & the classic failure
When a model looks broken but the tokenizer is the culprit
slides.body: Symptom family: a model that is fine on ordinary English suddenly degrades on emoji, rare Unicode, a new language, or a new domain — *with weights unchanged*. Mechanism: out-of-distribution characters have no learned merges, so they shatter into many byte-level fallback tokens; the input becomes a long, low-signal sequence the model never trained on. The fix is at the tokenizer (broader/byte-level coverage, or domain-matched vocab), not the weights. Recognizing "this is a tokenization problem, not a model problem" is a senior-level diagnostic skill. Practice it:

question.question: Diagnose the tokenization failure.
question.scenario: A model trained on English text suddenly performs terribly on user input full of emoji and rare Unicode symbols. The tokenizer and vocabulary are unchanged.

rubricCriteria.description: rare/unseen characters fragment into many subword or byte fallback tokens
the sequence balloons / meaning is diluted across many tokens
fix: broaden tokenizer coverage (e.g. byte-level BPE) or retrain the vocab

question.explanation: Out-of-distribution characters have no merged tokens, so they shatter into many tiny tokens — long, low-signal sequences the model never trained on.

hints: What corpus was the BPE vocab trained on?
Rare/unseen substrings have no merged token.
slides.workedSolution: BPE's merges come from frequent pairs in training text (mostly prose). Code symbols are rare there, so they remain unmerged subwords — more tokens for the same word count.

question.question: A 10-word English sentence becomes ~12 tokens, but a 10-word code snippet becomes ~40. Why?
options: Code has many rare substrings the BPE vocab never merged, so it fragments into more subword tokens
The model is simply larger for code
Code uses more characters per word, nothing else
question.explanation: BPE merges frequent pairs from its (mostly prose) training corpus; code identifiers/punctuation are comparatively rare, so they stay split into many short tokens.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body: Tokens are the atoms every later concept manipulates: attention mixes token vectors, the FFN transforms them, the LM head predicts the next *token*. You now know why the representation is subword and why the choice has quadratic cost consequences. Next: **BPE** — the exact greedy algorithm that *constructs* the vocabulary you just relied on, plus the precise vocab-size ↔ sequence-length tradeoff in numbers.
